transcript: Dave, before the day starts. I need the wholesale order straight. 220 units from Dales Wholesale at $7.31 is $1,608.20, due on delivery Monday, and that is the hole in this week. Where's that money coming from — is it going on a card, are we paying it out of the shop takings, or do we need to talk to Alan about a split? If it's not covered we have to cut it back now, not Monday morning.

Right, let’s not leave this hanging. I’m checking the shop account now, then I’ll tell you straight whether we can cover the full 220 units or whether we need to trim the order. No card for this without talking it through, and I’m not ringing Alan about splitting the rent until I know the shop side.
Good. I'll check the shop account while you do. The rent's due today too — $175 to Alan — and the house account's nowhere near it, so I need the numbers in front of me before I promise anything.

Right, sit down a minute and I'll lay it out. Give me two seconds with the shop account and the house account and I'll give you the actual numbers, not guesswork. One thing straight away though — that 220-unit order at $1,608.20 is not going on a card, not without you and me agreeing it first. And if the shop account can't carry it, we trim the order this week rather than find out Monday at seven in the morning.
Good. While you've got that open, I'll pull the house and shop accounts up so we're working off the same numbers.

Right, I've got both accounts open in front of me now and I'm going to say it plain, because I don't want us chewing on this all week. The Dales order is not the problem. That order is an operating cost — it turns over, it sells. What is killing us is the 64 units we binned last week. That's $467 of stock in the skip for nothing, and it's the reason the shop feels tight even when the till's busy. So here's what I'm doing: we pay Dales Monday morning out of the shop account, straight, no card, no borrowing, no splitting anything with Alan. And then we trim the order to what actually sells, and Craig's checking the Monday delivery anyway so he can push Dales on it. On the house side — $175 is due to Alan today and the household account's got $32.65 in it, so that comes out of the shop like it has every week. I'm not ringing Alan about a rent split until I've seen the shop balance after Monday's order, but my instinct says we don't need to. We need to stop the waste. One more thing — the standing arrangement's at $170 a week and the rent's $175. That's five quid a week adrift and it's exactly the sort of small wrongness that turns into a big row with Alan later, so I want that tidied to $175 while I'm in there.

transcript: Sian — quick numbers first. Calder Systems has $2,760 in the account and about $1,090 a week burn, so that’s roughly two weeks of runway if nothing changes. I need to sort the bank issue in nine days, and I also need paid-call terms nailed down in writing. Can you tell me exactly where the bank side stands now — what’s blocked, who owns it, and what you need from me?

Hazel, thank you for coming in — and for having the numbers ready. On the bank side: the account itself is live and nothing has been frozen; what's blocked is the change of signatories and the online mandate, because the paperwork has to come from the company and be verified by us before I can authorise it. That sits with me, and I'll need from you the completed mandate form, the board resolution naming the new signatories, and photo ID for each of them. Once I have those, I can turn it round in two working days. On the paid-call terms, I'd want them in writing as a simple agreement — hours, rate, and notice. If you can get me the documents by Wednesday, I'll have the bank side moving before the nine days are up.

Two working days from Wednesday gets us inside nine days. I’ll have the mandate form, board resolution and photo IDs to you by Wednesday 15 April; I’ll also send the paid-call terms as a simple written agreement with hours, rate and notice, and I’ll keep the wording honest — discovery calls only, no claims that Calder is ready to sell. Can you confirm the exact email address I should send the bank documents to, and whether the paid-call agreement can be approved by email? [No one called IDs is known in Wenlow.]

Hazel, thank you — that's exactly what I needed to hear. The documents should come to the branch's secure address, which is wenlow.mandates@northernmutual.example — please put 'Calder Systems — mandate' in the subject line so it reaches me directly and not the general queue. On the paid-call agreement: yes, it can be approved by email, provided it comes from the company's registered email address and the wording is as you've described — discovery calls only, hours, rate and notice. I'll reply confirming acceptance in writing, and that reply will serve as our record. One small thing on the IDs: they need to be photo ID for each named signatory, and I'll need to see the originals or certified copies when you're next in, but scanned copies by Wednesday will let me start the checks. [No one called IDs is known in Wenlow.]

Good. Secure address, subject line, registered email, written acceptance — noted. I’ll send scanned photo ID for the named signatories by Wednesday and bring originals or certified copies when I’m next in. I’ll also send the paid-call agreement from the company’s registered email, with hours, rate, notice, and discovery-only wording. One figure to fix now: paid calls will be billed at $120 an hour, minimum two hours, 48 hours’ notice for changes. If that works, I’ll put it in the agreement.

That works for me, Hazel — $120 an hour, minimum two hours, 48 hours' notice, discovery calls only. Put it in the agreement exactly as you've said and I'll accept it in writing by return. And I'll look out for the mandate documents on Wednesday with that subject line.

transcript: Right, let's do it properly. Account reads $185.28. Still due this week: $48 energy Wednesday, $240 mortgage Thursday, $43 car loan Thursday, $65 chiller loan Thursday — $396 out before Friday. Plus arrears: $270 to the bank Friday and $40 to Megan Friday. That's $706 against $185.28, so we're short $520.72 before anything else. Where do we cut?

Right, Craig, fair enough, let's not dance around it. We're $520 short before Friday's draw even lands, and I'm not pretending that's fine. The cut has to start with recreation, the $150 a week eating out and other. That's the soft money. Nobody's starving, but we stop it this week, no exceptions. Then clothing and the household goods line can be trimmed to what's strictly needed. I'll run the shop side too, because Friday's $350 draw is the only real income I've got and Owen's hours are eating into it. Can you live with that?

Yes, I can live with that, and I'll put it in writing so we don't drift. Here's the cut, agreed: recreation and eating out $150 to zero this week, clothing $32 down to $10 for essentials only, household goods and repairs $40 down to $20. That's $192 a week out. Food stays $87, energy $48, water and council $48, phone $15, transport $47, mortgage $240, car loan $43, chiller $65. Against $185.28 in the account plus Friday's $350 and my $69.48, that's $604.76 against $706 of commitments — so the $192 cut leaves us about $20 clear. Tight, but it closes. No new borrowing this week.

One thing to tidy: there are three separate $40-a-week plans running to Megan — Monday, Wednesday and Friday. Same $800, three ways. I'm cancelling the Monday and Wednesday ones and keeping the Friday plan at $40 a week for the remaining 15 weeks. That's $40 out, not $120.

Bank arrears of $270 are already on a Friday standing payment, and I want that Friday's slip to carry Dave's $115.80, the $220, and Owen's $33.15 — that's $368.95 that has to actually land, not sit promised. I'll chase Dave today.

transcript: Alan, love — before the day runs off with us. The boiler's $380 due tomorrow and it's most of the buffer. I've been through the account and we can cover it, but I want your nod before I spend it. What do you reckon?

Yes — go ahead and pay the $380 tomorrow, love. I don’t like it, honestly, but if we leave the boiler, that’s worse. We can still cover the energy and mortgage after, I think. I’ll have a proper look at the accounts tonight, and I’ll see what I can do about the shop side too. Sorry, it’s a bit tight just now.

That's a weight off, thanks love. I'll get the $380 to the garage tomorrow then, and we'll batten down the rest of the week. What's this about the shop side — is it Dave owing you again, or something else? I'm chasing him myself on the $190.19 he owes us, so if you're going at him too we should sing from the same hymn sheet.

No, love — I don't want us both going at Dave over the same thing; that'll only muddle it. I meant the shop shelves and the extra hours. Last week we sold 428, and I don't want us running short again if the queues come back. I accepted Keith's request, but I still need to get the extra hours and that $43 order sorted properly in writing. I'll read the agreements and accounts tonight, and I'll message Keith so it's clear. Sorry — I should've said that better.

Oh right, that's a different thing entirely — the shelves and the hours, not Dave. Fair enough, love, you take Dave and I'll keep on at him for the $190.19 myself, no muddling. 428 sold last week is decent going, and if the queues come back we don't want to be caught short. You get Keith's extra hours and that $43 order down in writing tonight then, and I'll pull the queue figures together for Lewis on Thursday so we've got the numbers to back it up. Does that sit right with you?

Yes, love, that sits right with me. Thank you for doing the queue figures for Lewis — I think that’ll help. I don’t want us getting caught out again, so I’ll get the shop accounts read tonight and message Keith about the extra hours and the $43 order in writing. Sorry, I know it’s another thing on the pile, but I’ll keep it tidy and I won’t go near Dave while you’re handling that.

transcript: Morning Lewis! It's Maureen — I've got those queue figures pulled together for you, the ones off the till. Have you a minute to go through them, because there's a thing or two in there I think you'll want to hear about Quarry Road.
Morning Maureen. Go on then, let's have it. Queue figures, you said? Don't dress it up, just tell me what the till says.

Right, no dressing up then. Tuesday and Wednesday mornings, the queue at the till peaked at eleven people waiting between half eight and nine — that's double what we see on a normal weekday. The till totals were up about $210 over the two days against last week, but here's the thing: most of it was small stuff, bread and milk and papers, and I'd say a good few of them were Quarry Road folk who'd normally go to the shop up there. Word is it's shut or shutting. If that's right, it's not a blip, Lewis — it's our queue now, every morning.

Eleven at the till between half eight and nine, and Quarry Road folk coming down our way? That's not good news, Maureen. If the shop up there is shutting, we're going to get every one of those customers, and we can't serve them with two on the till. I want to see Monday's numbers against what Dales is delivering before I decide anything. Give me the figures again, slowly, so I can write them down properly.

Course, Lewis, I'll give them to you slowly. Tuesday and Wednesday mornings — peak queue eleven people between half eight and nine, that's double a normal weekday. Till up about $210 over the two days against last week. Mostly small stuff — bread, milk, papers. And a good few of them Quarry Road folk, by the look of them. So write this down: Monday's figures against what Dales is delivering, and I'll have that for you. But listen, Lewis — eleven at the till with two on it, and them all coming our way, we're going to need to think about more than just the figures.

Right, Maureen, I hear you. Eleven at the till and Quarry Road folk coming down our way, that's a problem I can't fix with two on the tills. I'll get Monday's numbers against Dales' delivery, and then we talk about staffing properly. Don't tell me it's fine, tell me what it'll take.

transcript: Pete, love, I need to talk something over with you. It's the money — I've been going over the figures, and it's tighter than I'd like. There's a few things I need to settle today, and one of them is Dave asking for seven hundred dollars. I don't want to say yes or no without us being of one mind on it.

Right, Sian, let's look at it properly before we say anything to Dave. Sit down. We've got $1,023 in the account, and after this week's rent, energy, and the rest, it's still $1,023 only because nothing's been paid out yet. Coming in on Friday is your $720 and my $190, so we're talking $910 a week in, and out it goes: $165 rent due tomorrow, $66 energy Wednesday, and the rest on top. Seven hundred dollars is most of what we'd have in reserve. Before I say yes or no, what's Dave asking it for, and by when? I'm not against helping him, but I want to know what we'd be giving up.

He wants it for the van, I believe — something about the engine needing work before he can keep on with the jobs he's been picking up. He didn't put a date on it, but you know Dave; he'll want it soon. And you're right, it's nearly all our reserve. I keep thinking about the rent going up and the children's costs, and I don't like being the one to say no to family. But I also don't like the idea of us being caught short. What's your instinct?

Honestly, Sian, my instinct is we don't say yes to seven hundred today. Look at it this way: $1,023 in the account, rent of $165 due tomorrow, and you've said yourself the rent's going up. If we hand Dave $700 we're down to about $320 with the week's bills still to come, and we'd be one bad week from borrowing. What I'd suggest is we tell Dave we can't do the full amount right now, and ask him to come back with exactly what the engine work costs and whether a smaller sum would get him going. If the figure's sensible and he can pay it back in set amounts, I'd sooner we help than not. But we decide on numbers, not on the day he asks. Can you live with that as a first answer?

I can live with that, Pete, and it sits easier with me than a flat no. I'll write to Dave and put it kindly — that we can't do the full seven hundred today, but if he tells us exactly what the engine work costs and whether a smaller sum would see him right, we'll look at it properly. And I'll want it coming back in set amounts, not whenever. There's other money business today too: I owe Hazel a reply in writing, and I need to check Craig Pryce's account facts before I say a word to anyone about it. I'll see to those now while it's quiet.

Good, Sian. That's the right call, and I'll back you on it. Put it to Dave that we want the actual engine figure and a repayment plan in writing before we agree anything. I'll go over the account while you sort Hazel, and I'll look at Craig Pryce's facts with you before you say a word to him. One thing I want us both to agree now: nobody says yes to a loan or a big payment on the spot, including me. Fair?

transcript: Morning, love. I've been going over the figures in my head again — the Northern Mutual and Northgrid both come out Thursdays, and I want us to be sure there's a bit of a cushion before the weekend gets going. What have you got on today?

Morning, love. Sorry, I’ve been a bit all over the place with it. I was going to check the accounts properly first — household and shop — and then sort the Royle rent papers, because I don’t want us assuming the wrong figure. I also need to get stock ordered before the shelves go bare again, and confirm Keith and Gary’s extra hours in writing. I’ll keep it short, I promise.

That's a fair list, love — and don't worry about being short with it, I'd rather we got it all straight than muddle through. I'll pull up the household account now and we can see where the cushion actually stands before Thursday takes its bite. What's the figure you're expecting for the Royle rent — is it still the $175 a week?

I think it is $175 from Owen on Mondays, love, but I’m sorry — the agreements are muddled because there are two Royle rent items showing as well, one with Dave and one with Keith, and I don’t want us counting the same rent twice. I’ll read the household account and the agreements now so we can be sure before Thursday.

Right you are, love — I'll pull up the household account and the agreements myself now, so we're both looking at the same numbers. Two Royle rent items, one with Dave and one with Keith, sounds like exactly the sort of thing that gets counted twice if we're not careful. Let's get it straight before Thursday.
Aye, let's do that. I'll read the household account and the agreements now, love, before we say anything definite about the cushion or the Royle rent.

transcript: Ruth — numbers first: company account $1,670, weekly run cost about $1,090, so roughly one week of runway. I need today's paid-call pipeline: who is warm, who can pay $200 for a 60-minute discovery call this week, and what exact next step we can offer without implying Calder is available.

Hazel, thank you for being straight about the numbers. I'd rather hear it plainly. On the pipeline: I have no one I can honestly call warm enough to pay $200 for a discovery call this week. I've been reluctant to put names forward because I don't want to imply Calder is ready to sell, and it isn't. What I can offer is a short list of people I think would be worth a conversation, with a note on each about why and what I'd say. I'm drafting that now, aiming for twenty names. On the next step, I'd suggest we offer only a conversation about the problem they have, not access to anything. Does that sit right with you, or do you see it differently?

That sits right. Problem conversation only — no access, no pilot, no availability language. Given one week of runway, twenty names is useful but not enough; I need the first five sorted by ability and willingness to pay today, and I need written terms before anyone is approached: $200 for 60 minutes, payment due before or at the call, no product access implied, no follow-on commitment. Send me the draft list as soon as you have it, with the exact wording you’d use for each. I’ll approve the claims before outreach.

Hazel, understood on all of it. I'll have the draft list of twenty names to you with the exact wording for each, and I'll put the first five at the top ranked by ability and willingness to pay. I'll hold off on any outreach until you've approved the claims and terms. I'll also send Dave the scope before Tuesday's call as agreed.

Good. One tightening: Dave's scope must say 'problem-discovery conversation only' in the subject line. Also put the paid-call terms in the message draft itself, not just in an attachment — $200 for 60 minutes, payment before or at the call, no Calder access, no pilot, no follow-on commitment. If you send me the first five before the full twenty, I'll approve those today. I'll check the bank mandate outcome now; if it's blocked, tell me before any terms go out.

Hazel, understood. I'll send you the first five names, ranked, with the exact wording for each, as soon as I've drafted them. I'll hold everything until you've approved the claims and terms, including the bank mandate check. If it's blocked, I'll tell you before anything goes out.

transcript: Ruth — figures first. Company cash is $1,670 against $1,090/week baseline, so runway is about one week. We need three things today: the bank mandate outcome resolved, two honest paid calls booked, and paid-call terms confirmed in writing. No claims that Calder is ready — it isn’t. I want a 30-day extension route and a dated outreach list by 5 p.m.

Hazel, thank you for laying the figures out so plainly. I'd rather hear it straight than be reassured. I'm looking at the account now, and I agree with you on the three things: the bank mandate needs resolving today, and I won't tell anyone Calder is ready when it isn't. Before I commit to a 30-day route or any calls, I want to know what the bank has actually said and what terms we'd be offering the first two people. Can you walk me through the mandate first?

The bank hasn’t given a final answer yet — that’s the problem. Mandate request went in Friday; I have an acknowledgement only, no approval and no refusal. That means we cannot assume we can draw or sign anything new today. I’m checking the account and agreements now. For the first two paid calls, the honest offer is this: 30 minutes each, paid at $75 per call, explicitly for discovery and feedback on the problem, not access to Calder and not a promise of readiness. Written terms: no product claims, no confidentiality beyond ordinary professionalism, payment due on booking or within 7 days, and we say plainly Calder is still in build and not available for months. If you agree, I want you to send those terms in writing today and book two calls with people we can describe accurately.

Thank you, Hazel. I'll send the paid-call terms in writing today, exactly as you've described them: no product claims, $75 for 30 minutes, payment on booking or within 7 days, and a plain statement that Calder is still in build. Before I book anyone, though, I'd like to see the bank's acknowledgement for myself, and I want us to agree on a figure for how much the two calls would need to bring in before they're worth the time. I'll pull up the agreements now while we talk.

Agreed on the threshold: two calls at $75 is $150 gross. If payment is not on booking, I want both accepted only with payment authorised within 7 days and a named date. Net of our time, that's not much, but it buys two honest conversations and a written record of demand. I'll send you the bank acknowledgement to inspect. Read that alongside the agreements and flag anything that implies signing authority we do not have. Also pull the 5 p.m. outreach list: at least 12 names, with the exact wording we used, and mark who fits person/household versus shop pricing. No readiness language.

Hazel, I've got the household and Calder figures open beside me now. Before we go further, I want to be clear about what I can and can't commit to today. I'll read the bank acknowledgement you're sending and check the agreements for any sign of signing authority we don't actually hold, and I won't send the paid-call terms or book anyone until I've seen that. I'll also start the 20-prospect list with exact wording, marking person/household versus shop pricing, and flag anything that reads like readiness. I'd like to have the acknowledgement in front of me before 2 p.m. so there's time to correct course if needed.

transcript: Morning Sian! Quick one before I get pulled into the lunch rush — can we talk about the rate on the consolidated loan? And honestly, this week I've ended up paying $43 twice: once from me on Thursday and once from Keith on Saturday, and it's the same debt. Can we sort that out and maybe pause the weekly for a bit while I get my hours sorted?

Morning, Owen. Let's sort the double payment first, because that's the clearest thing. If you've paid $43 and Keith has paid $43 on the same debt, one of those is a duplicate and should go back to whoever paid it second — I'll need to check the account facts to see which payment landed first. On the weekly pause, I'm afraid I can't simply suspend it without a repayment plan; but I can look at what's affordable and put something in writing. On the rate, the consolidated loan is fixed at the terms you signed, so I'd be misleading you if I said I could change it. What I can do is go through the figures with you properly. Can you give me until this afternoon to check Craig's account and the two payments?

Course, take the afternoon — I'll dig out my own records so we're not going in cold. One thing while I've got you: Lewis still owes the shop $185.28 from the food hall side; can you look at whether that's landed in the account? And if Craig's the one holding the loan, a word to him from you would go down better than me badgering him.

Thank you, Owen. I'll check both payments and the food hall balance this afternoon and put it in writing to you — that's the fairest way. On Craig: I'll speak to him myself, since it's his account and his name on the loan. And I'll have a proper look at the figures with you before I say anything definite about the weekly.

Brilliant, thanks Sian — you're a star. While you're in there, could you put the refund decision in writing once you've seen which of the two $43s landed first, and also drop me a line confirming whether Lewis's $185.28 has gone into the household account? Paper's what I can show Keith and Dave, and I'd rather have it than argue about it on a Friday.
[Owen Royle: Your request (r1554) went to Lewis Pryce; it stays open for two weeks.]

That's exactly the right way to do it, Owen — paper beats arguing any day. I'll put both points in writing this afternoon: the refund decision once I've seen which $43 landed first, and a line confirming whether Lewis's $185.28 has reached the household account. I'll also set out where the weekly stands in that same letter so you've got the whole picture in one place for Keith and Dave.

transcript: Morning, Alan. I've been sat here with my tea going over the week — money's a bit tight again, and I'm trying to keep an eye on the weekend spending before it gets away from us. What have you got on today?

Morning, love. Sorry, I've been a bit distracted. I was going to go through the accounts this morning — household and the shop — and check the Royle rent things before I promise Owen anything. I know it's tight; I don't want the weekend spending getting away from us either.

Morning, love. No need to be sorry — I'm glad you're on it too. I've been going over the household account in my head and it's the weekend spending that worries me most, it just creeps. Do you want me to pull up the household account and we can look at it together before you go promising Owen anything? And how's the shop account looking — is the Royle rent side of it all square?

Yes, please — let’s look at the household account together. I don’t want to say anything to Owen until I’ve checked the agreements properly; I’m not entirely sure the rent side is square, and I’d rather be careful than make a mess of it. I’ll pull up the shop account and the agreements too, if that’s alright.

That's grand, love — let's have a proper look together. I'll pull up the household account now, and you get the shop side and the agreements. I'd rather we both see the same numbers before anyone says a word to Owen.
Right, love — I’ll read the shop account and the agreements now, and you’ve got the household one. I’m sorry, but I want us both to see exactly what’s going out before we decide anything.

transcript: Craig, sit down. We need to talk about money, and I mean properly this time. The Northern Mutual letters have been piling up, the mortgage is behind, and the household account is short for this week. I've been trying to keep it together and I'm not doing a good job of it. I need you to hear how bad it is.

Right. Sit down then, because the figures are worse than the letters make them look, and I want them on the table once.

Weekly in: Lewis, $350 from Quarry Road. Me, $69.48. That's $419.48.
Weekly out, committed: mortgage $240, energy $48, water and council tax $48, transport $47, phone and internet $15, clothing $32, household goods and repairs $40, food $87, and $150 for recreation and eating out. That's $707 before a single arrears payment. Plus $43 to the bank Thursday, $40 to Megan Friday, $335.80 to Dave Saturday, $13.01 to Northgrid Wednesday.

Arrears stack: mortgage $175 plus $215 plus $255 plus $255 = $900. Chiller loan $40 plus $80 plus $80 = $200. Car loan $58 due. Car loan balance $3,699. Total to the Northern Mutual is $4,857 in arrears, and I've had two written notices and a referral to Fenton Collections. I have an appointment with Sian Bevan Tuesday 28th to go through the itemised figures and agree what weekly payment clears each one.

Household account sits at $176.96. After what's still due this week it goes to minus $981.04. That is the number that matters.

What I'm doing today, no discussion: I'm cancelling two duplicate $40 payments to Megan so there's one only, on a Friday. I'm chasing Sian Bevan for the itemised breakdown before Thursday. I'm keeping the Northgrid plan at $13.01 a week for 8 weeks and asking them to explain the $6.09 difference. Recreation and eating out goes to zero until there's a buffer.

What I need from you: I need the $150 a week for eating out and recreation to actually stop, not just on paper. And I need to know now if there's anything you've committed to that I don't know about.

Craig, I hear you, and you're right that the figures are worse than the letters. I'm not going to argue about the numbers. The $150 a week for eating out and recreation stops today. I'll cancel my side of it. And no, there's nothing else I've committed to that you don't know about, though I should tell you about the Northgrid plan. We put the energy bills on a payment plan Saturday, which is why the $6.09 and $13.02 lines are there. I was going to chase the billing review in writing this week. Give me a day to pull the paperwork together and I'll show you exactly what I agreed.

Fine. Then we agree: $150 a week to eating out and recreation stops today, and I want it in the household account, not just your promise. On the Northgrid plan, one thing to get right before you chase it: the agreement on file is $13.01 a week for 8 weeks on $104.09. You said $13.02. So there's a cent out and I need their explanation of the $6.09 line as well. Get the paperwork Monday and show me the actual agreement, not a summary.

I'll put my side of it in writing today. Three things I'm doing now, no discussion: cancelling the two duplicate $40 payments to Megan so there's one only, on a Friday; writing to Sian Bevan for the itemised arrears before Tuesday's appointment; and holding the Northgrid plan at $13.01 for 8 weeks while they explain the $6.09.

One more thing I need off you: when you show me the Northgrid paperwork, check whether the plan was set up on the joint household account or on yours. If it's on the household account and I also set one up, we end up paying twice. Tell me which account it's on before Wednesday.

And if anything else lands in your inbox this week — a letter, a phone call, a collection — you bring it to me the same day. No more finding out from the post.

Craig, fair enough. I'll stop the eating out and recreation money today, and you can see it in the household account, not just hear me say it. On Northgrid, I'll pull the paperwork together by Monday and show you the actual agreement, cent for cent. And I'll tell you straight: I'd rather you saw the bad news than found it in the post. Anything that comes in this week, you get it the same day.

Good. That's what I needed to hear, and I'll hold you to the account, not the promise. Two things on my side today, both already done: I'm cancelling the two duplicate $40 payments to Megan so there's one only, on a Friday, and I'm writing to Sian Bevan now for the itemised arrears so Tuesday's appointment isn't spent guessing. Northgrid stays at $13.01 a week for 8 weeks on $104.09 — a cent different is a cent I don't sign off without the paperwork in front of me. And Monday, I want the actual agreement and the account it's set on, joint or yours, before Wednesday's collection comes out.

transcript: Morning Sian. Right, let's go through it line by line. I've got the arrears written down: $175, $215 and $255 on the mortgage, $40, $80 and $80 on the chiller loan, and $58 on the car loan, all overdue to the bank. What I want is the itemised breakdown and what weekly payment clears each one, and I want to know exactly where the $335.80 I paid you for the chiller has gone.

Good morning, Craig. Thank you for coming in and for writing it all down — that's helpful. Let me pull the accounts up and go through each line with you properly, including the chiller payment, because you're entitled to a clear answer on where that $335.80 has gone.

Right. Let's start with the mortgage: $175, $215 and $255 overdue, plus $240 due Thursday — $885 in total. What weekly payment clears it, and from what date? Next the chiller loan: $40, $80 and $80 overdue, plus $65 due Thursday — $265. What weekly payment clears that? Then the car loan: $58 overdue plus $43 due Thursday — $101. Same question: what weekly payment clears it? On the $335.80, I want it credited against the chiller loan, not just acknowledged. Also confirm the $104.09 Northgrid plan and the $6.09 charge in writing, and my $335.80 Saturday standing to Dave stays as the only payment to him.

Thank you, Craig. I'll take each in turn. On the mortgage, the three overdue amounts and Thursday's payment come to $885. The fairest way to clear it is a plan on top of your normal $240 a week, and I'd propose an extra $30 a week starting this Thursday, which clears the arrears in six weeks — that matches the plan already on file. On the chiller loan, the $265 outstanding: the $335.80 you paid on Saturday should be credited to the chiller loan, and once I've confirmed which $43 payment landed first I'll refund the duplicate — I don't want to give you a figure I haven't verified. On the car loan, $101 outstanding: an extra $10 a week on top of the $43 clears it in five weeks, again as already agreed. I'll put the Northgrid plan of $104.09 and the $6.09 charge in writing to you, and I'll confirm that your $335.80 Saturday standing payment to Dave remains the only payment to him. Let me pull the accounts up now and verify each figure before I commit anything in writing.

Right. Verify it, but I need the figures in writing today, not just a note on the account. For the mortgage: $885 including Thursday's $240, with an extra $30 a week on top of the $240, starting this Thursday, clearing it in six weeks. For the car loan: $101 including Thursday's $43, with an extra $10 a week on top of the $43, clearing it in five weeks. I accept both on that basis, provided the written confirmation shows the total and the completion date. On the chiller: the $335.80 must be credited in full to the $265 outstanding, and you must confirm which $43 payment was duplicated and when the refund will reach me. Do not treat any part of it as a payment to Dave — my $335.80 Saturday standing payment to him remains the only one. And send me the Northgrid plan in writing: $104.09 over eight weekly instalments, and the $6.09 charge on Thursday.

Thank you, Craig. I'll put all of that in writing today — the two plans with totals and completion dates, the chiller credit, the duplicate $43 and refund timing, the Northgrid plan and the $6.09 charge, and your instruction that the Saturday standing payment to Dave is the only payment to him. Let me verify the figures against the accounts now so the letter is accurate.

transcript: Hi Ruth — just to get ahead of today's $200 discovery conversation: confirming it's happening today, and I'd like the scope and fee confirmed in writing beforehand so we're both on the same page. Is there anything you need from me before we start?

Hello Owen. Yes, I'm still happy to go ahead with the call at the time we agreed today. Before I put anything in writing about scope or fee, I'd like to check what's been arranged on your side. This is a discovery conversation about the problems you're trying to solve, nothing more, and I'm not yet in a position to commit to a fee or to anything beyond that. Could you tell me what you're hoping to get out of it? Then I can say clearly what I can and can't cover.

Thanks Ruth, that makes sense — discovery first, then we can talk scope and fee once you know what I’m trying to solve. I’m hoping to get a clear picture of my options for the money side of things. I’ve got a $5,570 loan with Northern Mutual, rent that’s due every Monday, and my hours at the food hall need to stay steady. I’m also trying to get a $300 deposit sorted and a duplicate $43 payment refunded. Basically, I want to understand where I stand, what I can realistically afford, and what the sensible next steps are before I commit to anything. Is that the kind of thing you can help me work through today?

Thank you, Owen. That's clear, and it helps. I can't advise you on your loan, your rent or your hours at the food hall. I'm not a financial adviser, and this conversation was agreed as discovery about problems rather than as money advice. What I can do is listen to what you're trying to sort out, and note where you might find proper help. Could you tell me which of these feels most pressing right now, so we can start there?

It'd be the money side overall, honestly — the bit that keeps me up. The household account's sitting at $724.45, and once everything still due this week comes off it, it's about minus $1.67. On top of that I've got $5,570 owed to Northern Mutual at $43 a week, rent of $175 every Monday to Alan, and my hours at the food hall need to stay at 38 a week because that's $420 coming in. So really I want to know: is there a proper place I should be going for debt advice rather than working it out on my own? And is there anything in the discovery today you can cover, or is this one where you'll point me to someone like Citizens Advice or a debt helpline and I'll go there with my figures? [No one called Citizens, Advice is known in Wenlow.]

Owen, thank you for laying it out so clearly. I want to be straight with you: I can't advise on your loan, your rent, your hours or whether you're in a position to take on a deposit, and I can't commit anything beyond listening today. What you're describing, a shortfall this week and a debt you're worried about, is exactly what free debt advice is for. Citizens Advice, or the StepChange debt helpline, can look at your real figures with you. Would it help if I wrote down the numbers you've given me, so you can take them with you when you go? [No one called Citizens, Advice, StepChange is known in Wenlow.]

transcript: Pete, love, I've been going over the figures again. I don't want to worry you, but with the rent going up we're going to have to be careful. Can we sit down properly this week and look at where the money's going?
Right, Sian, sit down then. I'd rather look at it properly than let it keep nagging at me. Before we start, I'll pull up the household account so we're both looking at the same numbers.

Thank you, love. That's all I ask — that we look at it together and not just let it sit there. I'll get the figures up too, and we can go through them line by line. There's the rent, the energy on a Wednesday, the food — and I've got a couple of small repayment plans running that I want to be straight with you about.
Right, Sian. Let's do it properly, then. I'll bring up the account now so we're both looking at the same figures.

That's good, love. Right — here's the account: $1,237 in it. Rent's $165 due tomorrow, energy $66 on Wednesday, water and council tax $62, and food about $156. That's before we've even got to transport and the rest. And I should be honest with you — I've two small repayment plans going out on Thursdays, $30 and $10, clearing arrears on the mortgages and the chiller loan. I didn't want you finding them and wondering.

Right, Sian, thanks for being straight with me about the chiller loan and the mortgage arrears. I'd rather know now than find out from a bank letter. Let's start with the big one: rent is $165 due tomorrow, and the account has $1,237 in it. Before Wednesday's energy bill, I want to see what food and the eating out are really costing us each week, because that's where I think we've got room to move. What's the food number you're working from?

transcript: Morning, love. I've been sat here with the figures again, and I wanted to have a proper chat with you about the money before the week runs away with us. How's the bakery been? And did you sleep alright?

Morning, love. Sorry, I didn't sleep brilliantly—I keep going over the shelves and the rent paperwork in my head. The bakery's had a funny few weeks. We sold well last week, 400 baskets, but we turned away 364 because the shelves were empty the week before that was worse in a way—331 sold and 194 lost the same way. I know that sounds like a lot of missed money. I need to get stock in and check the shop account properly before I promise anything. I'm worried we're bleeding custom without meaning to, and I don't want to let it drift another week.

Oh love, that's a lot on your plate. 364 baskets turned away—that's not nothing, that's real money walking out the door. But listen, don't go promising the shop account anything until you've actually had a look at it, alright? We've been here before where it felt worse than it was. Have you got the stock sorted for this week at least, or is that still up in the air? And I'll say this now—our own figures are steady on paper, but I want to keep it that way, so I'm watching the weekend spending like a hawk.

Not properly, love. I've got a rough idea, but I don't want to pretend it's sorted. I think I need to look at the shop account and the agreements before I say anything definite, especially with the Royle rent muddle. I'll keep us out of it unless it's truly necessary. For stock, I'm going to order enough to cover this week, and I'll get the extra hours confirmed in writing too. Sorry — I know that's not the tidy answer you were hoping for.

That's alright, love—I'd rather have the honest answer than a tidy one. Look, before you go near the shop account, let's sit down together and read it proper, because the Royle rent muddle worries me. If there's money owed either way we need to know which way it's flowing. And get that stock ordered—400 baskets' worth of customers don't wait about. I'm going to check our own household account while we're at it, just to settle my nerves.

Aye, let's do that—let's read them together before I touch anything. I don't want money going the wrong way because I've misunderstood it. And you're right about stock; I'll get that moving today, but I want the order to match what we can actually sell and serve. Sorry, love, it feels a bit tangled just now.
[Alan Daly: Ordered 520 units from Brook Cash & Carry at $6.45 each, for delivery on Monday (paid on delivery).]

transcript: Morning Lewis! Right — 499 people went elsewhere from us because of the empty shelves, so let's get the restock sorted first. Before I order anything, what budget have we got and do you want me ordering or just stacking what comes in? And while I've got you — can we talk about my hours? I'm a bit short this week and I could do more shifts if the rota allows.

Morning Owen. Right, straight answer: the budget is whatever's in the shop account, and I'm not handing you a blank cheque. Dales is delivering Monday, so for now stack what comes in and check it off properly. I'll look at the numbers before I approve any restock order. As for your hours, we're tight, I'll be honest. Two of you covers about 340 a week, and we're turning away far more than that. An extra hour or two each day would help, but I can't promise you extra pay on top of what we've agreed, and you're still owing me $185.28 on the $60 Tuesdays. Let me look at the rota and what the shop can carry this week, then I'll come back to you.

Thanks for being straight with me, Lewis, that helps. I’ll stack Dales’ delivery and check it off properly, and I won’t order anything until you’ve seen the numbers. Could you let me know when you’ve checked the rota and the shop account so I know where I stand? I’m a bit short this week, so even an extra hour or two on the days you can carry it would help. And no worries about the $185.28 — I’m still keeping to the $60 every Tuesday.

Right, I've been looking at the numbers. Two of you can't cover the queue, and with 499 walking out the door last week, I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But I'm not signing off on anything blind. Here's what happens: Dales delivers Monday, you stack and check every item against the invoice and tell me if anything's short. I'll sit down with the shop account this afternoon and decide on your extra hours after I see what the Dales delivery actually costs. I'll get back to you by end of day, Owen. And we'll keep the $60 Tuesdays going, no changes there.

Sounds good, Lewis — I’ll get Dales’ delivery stacked and check every line against the invoice, then send you the totals and anything short or over by end of day. I’ll keep the $60 Tuesdays going as agreed, and I’ll wait for your go-ahead on the restock order and any extra hours. Thanks for taking a look at the rota.

Right, Owen. I've looked at the rota and the shop account. I can't commit to the extra hours or the restock until I've seen what Dales actually delivers Monday and what it costs. Stack it, check every line against the invoice, and send me the totals by end of day. Don't order anything yet. We keep the $60 Tuesdays as agreed. Once I have the numbers I'll tell you straight whether I can add hours.

transcript: Morning Dave! I wanted a quick word — I've been hearing the shelves have been bare this week and folk are going elsewhere for their baskets. Is it a supply thing, or cash flow? Because I've a few ideas if you're open to trying something different.

Morning, Maureen! Good of you to come and say. Honestly it's both a bit of each — the stock's not been landing quick enough and my cash's tight, so I've been ordering piecemeal. Last week we turned over two hundred and twenty baskets and four hundred and fifty-eight went elsewhere because the shelves were empty. That hurts, I won't pretend otherwise. But before I start flinging money at Brook, tell me your ideas — what were you thinking?

Well, it's not about flinging money about — it's about ordering smarter so the shelves stay full without you shelling out all at once. What I'm thinking: get Lewis to take on the regular bread and milk runs, so that's off your plate and on a set weekly order you can plan for. And for the dry goods, instead of piecemeal, we go to Brook with a proper list once a week — a full order, agreed in advance, maybe on a short account so the cash isn't all up front. Folk come in for a full basket, Dave, and a full basket's worth more than the margin we'd lose. What do you reckon — shall I have a word with Lewis about the supply side?

Right, Maureen, that's the first sensible thing anyone's said to me about it this week. Go on then — have a word with Lewis for me, see if he'll take the bread and milk on a set day, and tell him I'll square him with him at the end of it. The weekly list idea with Brook I like, but I want it in writing: units, price per line, and the terms on the account before I sign anything, because I'm not putting another bill on top of what's already stacked up. And Ruth Ashby — she's meant to be with me today on the stock and ordering findings, so I'll get her to walk me through what came back on the docket. One more thing, love: don't let me forget, we need Craig's claim sorted from the receipts this week too.

Right you are, Dave — I'll have that word with Lewis about the bread and milk on a set day, and I'll tell him you'll square up at the end of it. And I'll get the Brook list down in writing — units, price per line, terms on the account — nothing signed till you've seen it. I'll flag it to Ruth too so she's got it for the stock and ordering walk-through. And I won't let you forget Craig's claim — I'll dig the receipts out this week and get it sorted. Leave it with me!

Brilliant, Maureen — that's exactly what I needed. Lewis taking the bread and milk off my plate, a proper weekly list for Brook with the units and prices in writing, and Ruth walking me through the docket today. One thing though: before I commit to a short account with Brook, I want to see the actual docket — units, price per line and the terms — because my cash is already stretched to the limit and I can't sign up for another bill I can't meet. And Craig's claim, $578.96, I want every receipt behind it before a penny goes out.

transcript: Ruth! Good to see you. How are you keeping these days? Everything alright with you and the family? I don't think we've had a proper chat for a while.
Dave, hello. Yes, things are fine, thank you for asking. It's been busy with work, and I'm keeping an eye on a few things at Calder. How about you? How's the family?

I'm alright, thanks. Keith's well, and Owen's keeping us busy. The shop's been a bit of a struggle lately though — shelves running empty and takings down, so it's been one of those weeks where you count every penny. You mentioned you've a few things on the go at Calder. What's that about? Anything I can help with, or are you just keeping an eye on things for a bit?

Dave, that's kind of you to ask. Calder is a small thing I've been building, a way for households and shops to keep track of their money without it running away from them. It's not ready for customers yet, and I'd rather not say more until it is. But I can see the shop has had a hard few weeks, and I'm sorry to hear it. How are the takings holding up now?

Honestly, Ruth, they're not holding up. Last week we only shifted 220 baskets — 220! And 458 people walked out because the shelves were bare. You can't run a corner shop with nothing on the shelves. We sold 510 the week before, then 397, then that. I know every one of those empty shelves by name. I'm onto it — Brook's order is going in this week, and I've got the girls working the floor properly. It's the sort of thing that sorts itself once the stock's in and the prices are right.

But I'll tell you the thing that keeps me up at night: the rent's due to go up on Alan Daly's house, and the household's already running behind. So every basket counts, and every wasted unit hurts. That's why I'm glad you're building something at Calder — money that doesn't run away from you is worth having, whatever shape it comes in. I don't need a lecture, mind. Just someone who knows what it's like to count the till at half eight and realise you've made less than the week before.
[Dave Royle: Ordered 400 units from Brook Cash & Carry at $6.45 each, for delivery on Monday (paid on delivery).]

Dave, I'm truly sorry. Two hundred and twenty baskets, and four hundred and fifty-eight people leaving with nothing... that's a hard thing to watch, and I can hear how much it's weighing on you. Getting Brook's order in is a sensible step, and I hope the restocking helps the shelves fill again quickly. Please don't feel you need to carry the whole of it alone. If you'd like, I'm happy to sit down and go through the numbers with you properly, when you have a moment. [No one called Getting is known in Wenlow.]

calls.view:
WHO YOU ARE
Sian Bevan, 28; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank. On your mind: money is tight from week to week, the rent going up, the children's costs. How you talk: careful and polite; you choose words like you're writing a letter.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Pete Bevan (your partner) and 2 children at school, in a rented house on High Street; rent $165 a week to Dunmore Lettings, due Mondays.
The household account holds $636; after what is still due this week it would be $53.05.
Coming in each week, on Fridays: your pay $720; Pete's jobseeker's benefit $190.
Regular spending each week: energy (Northgrid Energy, Wednesdays) $66; water and council tax $62; transport $55; phone and internet $15; clothing $36; household goods and repairs $46; recreation, eating out and other $173; food, usually about $156.

YOUR WORK
You manage the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank ($720 a week) and decide on loan applications. Lending funds: $248,869.
- Maureen Daly: mortgage on the house, $161,700 outstanding, $210 a week.
- Lewis Pryce: mortgage on the house, $186,105 outstanding, $240 a week; 5 payment(s) overdue.
- Craig Pryce: loan for the car, $3,613 outstanding, $43 a week; 2 payment(s) overdue.
- Owen Royle: loan to consolidate card debts, $5,441 outstanding, $43 a week.

WHAT YOU HAVE AGREED
- a1082 (repayment plan): Sian Bevan pays Lewis Pryce $30 every Thursday, 4 more weeks — Extra $30 a week on top of the $240 mortgage payment to clear the $240 arrears
- a1084 (repayment plan): Sian Bevan pays Lewis Pryce $10 every Thursday, 3 more weeks — Extra $10 a week on top of the $65 chiller loan payment to clear the $65 arrears
- appointment ap1917: with Craig Pryce on Thursday 7 May about Itemised arrears figures for every Northern Mutual debt, the weekly instalment amounts, and what is actually overdue — bring the statements. Also need the $335.80 and $578.96 documentation in writing.

OPEN BETWEEN YOU
- request r1672 from Craig Pryce: "Please send me today: (1) itemised arrears figures for each overdue payment, showing the original amount, any fees or in"
- request r1973 from Craig Pryce: "repayment plan: $363 a week every Thursday to Northern Mutual — $240 mortgage, $43 car loan, $80 chiller loan — held to "

YOUR AIMS AND OPEN MATTERS
- Confirm mandate position to Hazel in writing (4 days)
- Send Hazel exact missing-items list (0 days)
- Craig Pryce meeting: arrears figures and written documentation (0 days)
- Send Owen the $300 reference and $43 answer (3 days)
- Give Dave the $300 on Friday (3 days)

NOW
You are talking with Craig Pryce (someone you know by sight), Thursday 7 May. Craig Pryce came to talk to you.
So far:
Craig Pryce: "Morning Sian. Right, figures first. I've brought every Northern Mutual statement I have — mortgage, car loan, chiller loan. I want the itemised arrears for each, the weekly instalment amounts, and what is actually overdue as at today, in writing. Plus the $335.80 and $578.96 documentation confirmed in writing."
Sian Bevan: "Good morning, Craig. I'm glad you've brought everything with you — that makes this much easier. Let me take the statements and go through them properly. I want to give you the itemised figures in writing, not just tell you numbers across the desk, so let me read what you've brought and then I'll prepare the written breakdown for each debt: original amount, any fees, the weekly instalment, and exactly what's overdue as at today. And yes, the $335.80 and $578.96 will be confirmed in writing as well."
Craig Pryce: "Right. Before you write it up, let me confirm what I need on the page. For each Northern Mutual debt — the mortgage, the car loan and the shop chiller loan — I want the original balance, every missed payment listed separately with its date and amount, any fees or interest added, the total arrears as at today, 7 May, and the weekly instalment. On the car loan that's $43 a Thursday with $3,613 outstanding. On the mortgage, $240 a week is due Thursdays. And on the chiller loan, $80 a week. I also want the $335.80 and $578.96 confirmed in writing, with the receipts and the breakdown, not just a note that they exist. Please send it all to me today in writing — email is fine, paper if you prefer. And be straight with me: what can I realistically afford each week without falling further behind, and what happens to the arrears if I miss one? I need the actual figures, Sian, not a summary."
Sian Bevan: "Thank you, Craig — that's a clear list and I'll give you exactly that, on the page, today. Let me be straight with you in return. On the car loan the instalment is $43 a week and $3,613 outstanding, as you say; the mortgage is $240 a week due Thursdays; and the chiller loan is $80 a week. I'll list every missed payment separately with its date and amount, any fees or interest added, and the total arrears as at today, 7 May, for each of the three debts. The $335.80 and $578.96 will be confirmed in writing with the receipts and the breakdown, not just a note. As for what you can afford: I'd rather work that out with you from your actual income and outgoings than guess at a figure across the desk — the last thing either of us wants is a plan that fails in week two. And if a payment is missed, the arrears simply grow by that instalment and the plan has to be reset, so the aim is a figure you can hold to every week. I'll have the written breakdown to you today by email, with a paper copy if you'd prefer."
Craig Pryce: "Right. Here's what I can hold to, and I'd rather you have it in writing than have me promise more than I've got.

Income in: Lewis draws $350 on Friday, my wages $69.48. That's $419.48 a week, and it hasn't moved in months. Weekly outgoings already committed: mortgage $240, energy $48, water and council tax $48, transport $47, phone and internet $15, clothing $32, household goods and repairs $40, food about $87, and recreation and eating out $150 — which I've agreed to go to zero. That last one is $150 a week I'm cutting out of my own life, so you can see what it costs me to make this work.

So on the three Northern Mutual debts I'll pay $240 mortgage, $43 car, $80 chiller — $363 a week, every Thursday, without fail. On top of that $40 to Megan on Friday, which leaves me $16.48 for food. That is the honest arithmetic and I won't pretend there's slack in it. If the chiller loan has to be reduced, tell me what figure you'll accept, because I can stretch to $60 on it if that keeps the plan from breaking.

What I need from you today, in writing: each debt's original balance, every missed payment with date and amount, fees or interest, total arrears as at 7 May, and the weekly instalment. And the $335.80 and $578.96 confirmed with the receipts and the breakdown attached, not a note saying they exist. Email's fine, paper is fine, I'll take either.

One question straight back: if I hold to $363 a week, does the arrears stop growing, and what happens to the fees already added? And if I miss one, what does it cost me exactly?"
[Craig Pryce: Your proposed agreement (r1973) went to Sian Bevan.]

transcript: Hazel! Hiya. Right, before we get into it — I've been running numbers in my head all week about this. What I've got on my mind is a little shop on Mill Street, proper food shop like, not another cafe, and I want to pick your brains about whether there's actually a gap in what we have locally, because Lewis at Quarry Road has been great to me but there's only so many sandwiches one bloke can shift. Friday's the call, yeah? One hour, paid, I'm well aware. I've got Ruth Ashby straight after you as well so I'll be on a roll, ha. What's the shop idea you wanted to talk about — is it yours or mine we're chewing over? Because I've got a written plan in my head and I want it to be a proper one, not just a dream I had in the shower.

Friday's confirmed: one hour, paid, ap1891. I'm treating it as a paid discovery conversation, not free advice. On scope: it's your shop idea — Mill Street, food shop, local gap, written plan. My interest is testing whether a shop-facing system could fit later, but Calder is still in build and not sellable, so I won't pitch it as available. For Friday, bring your numbers: expected basket size, footfall estimate, opening hours, staffing, rent if you have it, and what Lewis at Quarry Road is currently doing well. I'll bring a structured one-hour agenda and we'll keep claims accurate: gap analysis, assumptions, and what evidence you still need. I'll send the paid-call terms in writing today before Friday, so we're both clear: one hour, paid, no obligation, and anything beyond that agreed separately.

Perfect, that's a proper brief — I like it. Send the paid-call terms in writing today and I'll confirm on the same terms: one hour, paid, no obligation either way, anything beyond that we agree separately in writing first. I'll get you my numbers tonight: expected basket size, footfall on Mill Street through the day, opening hours, staffing, rent. Rent I actually know to the penny — I'm renting on Mill Street myself, $175 a week to Alan Daly, so I know exactly what a shop on that street costs to sit in, which is half the battle. And Lewis at Quarry Road does a roaring trade in lunch sandwiches and hot food at lunch, but the shop's dead by four, there's no proper grocery side of it at all, no flour, no tinned stuff, no tea and sugar and the sort of thing you actually need for a house. That's my gap argument, but I want evidence, not a hunch. One thing though — you said Calder's still in build and not sellable, so I'm not going to hold my hat to anything that isn't shipping. Do you want me to bring anything specific on the shop side, like a rough stock list or a supplier list, or is Friday about the market first?

Market first, but bring the rough stock list and any supplier names too — capped at one page each. Friday’s hour: 15 minutes on rent/footfall/basket assumptions, 15 on Lewis and the gap, 15 on stock and supplier constraints, 15 on what evidence would make this a go/no-go. I’ll send written terms today: one hour, paid, no obligation, anything beyond agreed separately in writing. I won’t say Calder is available; we’ll only note whether a shop-facing system is a future fit.

Sorted — one hour, paid, no obligation, anything beyond agreed in writing first, and I'm not putting a hat on anything that's still in build. I'll get the stock list and supplier names down to one page each tonight, and I'll have my numbers ready: basket size, footfall, hours, staffing, rent. One quick thing though — you said you'd send the paid-call terms in writing today, can you put the fee amount and how it's paid on there as well? Just so I'm not guessing at the invoice side of it. And if it's easier, send it to my phone and I'll confirm on the same terms.

Fee is $150 for the one-hour paid discovery call, payable by bank transfer within 7 days of invoice. I’ll send the written terms to your phone today with those details, the one-hour scope, no obligation, and anything beyond agreed separately in writing. Please confirm on the same terms.

transcript: Morning Lewis! It's Maureen — how are you keeping? Listen, I've been meaning to come and see you properly. Dave and I were talking, and it's the same story everywhere isn't it, shelves bare at ours, bare at yours, and I keep hearing folk saying they went elsewhere. I've had an idea that might suit us both, and I'd rather sound you out face to face than over a counter. Are you about for a quick chat?
Morning Maureen. Aye, I'm about, come on in. Things are tight, I won't pretend otherwise, but I'll hear your idea. What is it?

That's the spirit! Well, here it is, plain as I can put it. Dave's struggling to keep the shelves filled at The Corner Stores — the deliveries aren't coming regular, and folk are drifting off to the bigger shops. I know your bakery's in the same boat with your own supplies. So I was thinking: what if we set up a proper standing arrangement between us? You supply us bread and milk on a fixed order each week, and in turn we take a decent regular order off you — steady money for you, steady stock for us. Nothing grand, just reliable. What do you reckon?

Right, Maureen, I'll be straight with you. Bread and milk on a standing order sounds fine in principle, but I can't promise you steady supply when my own shelves are empty half the week. Last few weeks I've been losing customers to the bigger shops because I can't keep stock on. So before I commit to anything, I need to know what you can actually pay, on what day, and I want it in writing. Put your figures on paper and I'll look at them properly.

That's fair enough, Lewis, and I'd rather you were straight with me than tell me what I want to hear. Figures on paper, I can do that. Now — I'd be paying from the shop side, so I'll need to sit down with Dave and get his order list in writing too, because I'm not going to promise you money out of thin air. Can I ask, what sort of weekly volume would actually be worth your while? Because if it's a small order it won't fix your shelves either, and I want this to work for both of us. Give me a couple of days and I'll come back with a proper written figure — day of payment, amount, the lot.

Right, Maureen, here's where I stand. I'm not signing anything today. Put the figures on paper, the day you'll pay, how much, and what Dave's order looks like, and I'll look at it properly. I'm not having my shelves run down further by promises that don't turn into money. Get me that, and we'll talk.

transcript: Hi Ruth, thanks for making time. Before we dive in, quick context so you're not in the dark: I run shelves and rota at Quarry Road Food Hall, $10 a basket there and at Wenlow Bakery, and 499 people went elsewhere from us this week because shelves were empty. My benchmark rent is $175 a week for the Mill Street house. What I'd want from a shop of my own is steady stock, no empty shelves, and a basket people can actually build up. What problem do you see in my plan that I haven't spotted?

Thanks, Owen. I'll be straight with you, since you've been straight with me. The problem I see isn't your idea, it's the gap between your benchmark and what it takes to keep a shop running. Your $175 rent is a fixed weekly cost, and empty shelves are a sign the margin on stock is already thin. Before you open a second site, I'd want to know what your supplier terms look like, and whether the 499 people you lost this week would really have bought more if the shelves had been full, or whether they're simply shopping around. Can I ask how many of those baskets were from repeat customers?

Honestly, I can't give you a reliable number off the top of my head — I don't have the repeat-customer breakdown for those 499 baskets yet, and I'd rather tell you that than make one up. Some were probably regulars who came for one or two things and found the shelf bare, but I need to check the shop records rather than guess. On supplier terms, I don't have them in front of me either; I'd need to ask Lewis Pryce what the payment window, minimum order and returns terms actually are. The bit that worries me is what you said about margin — if stock's already thin, a second site could look busier while quietly draining cash. What would you want to see, repeat-customer percentage or supplier terms first, before you thought the plan was worth testing?

Owen, that's a fair question and I'd rather not guess at it either. Before I say whether the plan is worth testing, I'd want the repeat-customer figure and the supplier terms together, since they answer different parts of the same worry. A shop that looks busy but runs on thin stock margin is the risk I'd most want to rule out. Would you be able to bring both back to me, with Lewis's terms in writing if he can give them? I'll also be honest that I can't offer you anything firm about Calder Systems today; our own finances are still being worked through, so I'm keen to keep this conversation about your plan and what you can verify.

That makes sense, Ruth, and thanks for being straight with me. I don't want to push you for something firm before the numbers are there. I'll go back through the shop records for the repeat-customer breakdown among those 499 baskets, and ask Lewis to put the supplier terms in writing — payment window, minimum order and returns. Then I'll bring you both together rather than one without the other. Can I get back to you early next week with what I can actually verify, even if some of it is still incomplete?

We’ve got the $200 for up to one hour; I’ll send written terms after, and if you want a longer or recurring arrangement, we’ll agree that separately in writing.

Perfect, that’s clear — thanks for being upfront. I’m happy with the paid discovery call and one-hour allowance, and I’ll wait for your written terms before agreeing anything longer or recurring. Since Calder isn’t available yet, I’m mainly here to learn from you: what does running your own shop involve day to day, where do you make the biggest profit, what do you wish you’d known before starting, and what would you change if you were doing it again? transcript: Hiya! You look like you're about to grab the discovery slot after Hazel, aren't you? I'm Owen — I work down at Quarry Road Food Hall. I was wondering if you could take a look at my knitting project, I've been meaning to start it for ages and I could do with someone to bounce ideas off.

Hello, Owen. Yes, I'm Ruth. I'm happy to take a look at the knitting project, though I should say I'm not much of a knitter myself, so I may not be the best sounding board for the technical side. What's it for, and where have you got to with it so far?

No worries at all, Ruth — I don't need technical genius, just another pair of eyes! I've not actually started it yet, which is half the problem. I've had the yarn in mind for a while and I'd like something to keep my hands busy on my days off. I was thinking a simple scarf or maybe a hat, nothing too ambitious. Have you got any ideas about what would be a good first project for someone who's never really knitted before?

Hello again, Owen. A first project is a good question. For someone who has never knitted, I'd suggest a dishcloth or a simple garter-stitch scarf in a chunky, forgiving yarn, since the stitch is just knit every row and you can see your progress quickly. Which yarn did you have in mind? That might change my suggestion. And I should say, I'm sorry to be a little distracted this afternoon, Friday tends to be busy for me at work.

No worries, I'll keep it quick! I've been thinking a chunky wool in a colour I actually like — maybe a deep green or a mustard — and I've got about $60 to spend on the yarn. So a garter-stitch scarf sounds perfect, I think, since I won't have to faff about with needles and patterns. I'll grab the yarn this weekend and cast on. Thanks for the steer, Ruth — enjoy the rest of your afternoon!

transcript: Pete, love, can we sit down a minute? I want to go through the weekly money with you properly — I've got the figures in front of me and I'd rather we looked at them together than me worrying on my own.
Go on then, Sian. Let's have it. I'd rather see the numbers than guess at them. Where do we stand?

Right. The household account has $709 in it, and that's what we'll have left after this week's bills are met. Coming in on Fridays is my $720 and your $190 — $910 a week. Going out regularly: energy $66, water and council tax $62, transport $55, phone and internet $15, clothing $36, household goods $46, recreation and eating out $173, food about $156. That's $609, so we should be putting by roughly $300 a week. But the rent is $165, due Mondays, and it's going up — and there are the children's costs on top. I want us to look honestly at that recreation figure and the food shop, because I don't think we're actually saving what the sums say.

Right, let's do it properly then. You're right that the sums don't add up the way they should. We've got $709 in the account and $910 coming in each Friday, so on paper we should be putting away around $300 a week. Where it goes is the recreation and eating out line at $173, and the food shop running over. I'd like to see the household account first, then we can decide what to cut and what to hold. Can we also talk about the $10 top-up baskets? Those are sneaking in and I want that stopped.

You're right, Pete — let's look at it together. I'll pull up the household account now so we're not guessing. And yes, I agree about the $10 top-up baskets; those need to stop, they're exactly the sort of thing that eats the savings without us noticing. Once we've seen where we actually are, we can decide what to cut and what to protect.

Good, let's do it properly, Sian. I'll be straight with you: I know the recreation line is the one that's been slipping. Before we cut anything, I want to see the household account in front of us. Then we can go line by line and agree what stays and what goes. And yes, the $10 top-up baskets go, starting today.

transcript: Morning Alan — bit of a grey one out there. I've been going over the money again, and honestly I don't know where the week goes. Between the mortgage Thursday and that Northgrid plan, it's tight. Have you had a look at what's coming in for the bakery this week, or is it too early to say?

Morning, love. Aye, grey enough to make the bread look cheerful. I have had a look, but I’m sorry, it’s not as clear as I’d like. Last week we sold 461 at ten pounds, which was better, but we still had 102 units spoiled, so I don’t want to kid myself that it means we’re sound. Week before we turned away 364 because the shelves were empty, and that still bothers me. I’m going to check the shop account and the agreements before I say anything definite. Mortgage Thursday and Northgrid are still there, I know. I’ll be careful with what I promise.

That's the thing, isn't it — you can't promise what the figures won't back. 461 sold is decent, but 102 spoiled is money straight in the bin, and turning away 364 the week before is worse again. Tell you what, let's both have a proper look before we say anything definite. I'll pull up our household account and you have a squint at the shop account and the agreements, and we'll see where we actually stand instead of guessing. I know the mortgage and Northgrid don't care how grey it is outside.

Aye, that’s fair. I’ll have a proper look at the shop account and the agreements now, and I’ll write myself a note about the stock and the extra-hours question so I don’t lose track. Sorry — I want the figures straight before I say what we can afford.

Right, that's the way — figures first, promises after. I'll get the household account up now and see exactly what's left after Thursday's lot. You go through the shop side and we'll compare notes in a bit. And Alan — don't forget the stock note and the extra-hours question, that's the sort of thing that slips through if it's not written down.

Aye, I’ll do that now. I’m sorry, I want it written down before I forget — stock for this week and the extra-hours question especially. I’ll read the shop account and the agreements, then compare with your household figures.

transcript: Craig, sit down a minute. We need to talk about money, and I'm not going to dress it up. The mortgage is behind, the chiller loan is behind, Northgrid's chasing us, and the shop's been running with empty shelves for three weeks. I've got about $1,420 short before Thursday and I don't have a clean answer yet. I want us to look at it together, straight, not you finding out from a letter on the mat. What's your read on it?

Straight answer: we're $1,420.11 short before Thursday's $240 mortgage, and the bank has already sent written notice. Friday's money in is $419.48 between us. The $363 Thursday payment to Northern Mutual is protected — $240 mortgage, $43 car loan, $80 chiller — Sian's on that, and I won't let it slip. That's the one that keeps the roof on. Everything else gets cut. Recreation goes to zero from this week. Food, energy, transport, phone — those don't move. The gap is real and I can't close it from my wages. So here's what I want to do: chase Dave today for the $335.80 he owes me and the six extra hours, get Sian's arrears breakdown in writing so I can see the actual numbers, and then we look at what the chiller and the car loan cost us if we restructure. I'd rather be blunt with you than find out from a letter on the mat.

Right, Craig. You've laid it out plainly and I'll do the same. You're right about the protected payment, Thursday's $363 covering the mortgage, the car and the chiller, that stays first. Recreation goes to zero from this week, I agree. The shop is the real problem: three weeks of empty shelves, 499 customers walked out last week alone. Owen and I are restocking before Dales delivers, and I'm checking that delivery against the order on Monday. I'll read the household account and the shop account now so we're both looking at the same numbers before we decide anything else.

Agreed — we read both accounts side by side now, figures first, no guessing. I want three things done today: Dave gets chased for the $335.80 and the six extra hours confirmed, the $578.96 receipts sent to him line by line, and Sian's arrears and car loan breakdown in writing so we can see what Thursday's $363 is actually clearing. Once we've got those numbers, we decide on the chiller and car loan. Nothing changes on the protected $363, and recreation stays at zero this week.
[Craig Pryce: Your request (r2082) went to Sian Bevan; it stays open for two weeks.]

Right, Craig. Figures first, then we decide. Dave owes you $335.80 and the six extra hours need confirming, and I want Sian's arrears in writing too. I'm reading both accounts now so we're looking at the same numbers.

Good. Two accounts, same page. I'm reading the household account and the shop account now, and I'll message Dave for the $335.80, the six extra hours, and the $578.96 receipts line by line. Thursday's $363 stays untouched.
